items.prose: Take $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ about $a = 9$, so $f'(x) = \tfrac12 x^{-1/2}$ and $f''(x) = -\tfrac14 x^{-3/2}$.
items.question: Write the quadratic approximation of $\sqrt{x}$ about 9, in powers of $(x - 9)$.

widget.label: Quadratic approximation of root x about 9

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate $f$, $f'$ and $f''$ at 9, then halve $f''(9)$.

byKey.no-half: $-\tfrac{1}{108}$ is $f''(9)$. The coefficient is half of it.
byKey.sign: $\sqrt{x}$ bends down, so the square term is negative.
byKey.old-centre: $-\tfrac18$ is the coefficient for $\sqrt{1 + x}$ at 0. Evaluate at 9: $9^{-3/2} = \tfrac{1}{27}$.

items.question: Estimate $\sqrt{10}$ to 5 decimal places.

explain.text: $3 + 0.16667 - 0.00463 = 3.16204$. The true value is 3.16228, so the error is 0.00024, against 0.0044 for the tangent.

items.prose: Derive the series for $(1 + x)^{\alpha}$, for any power $\alpha$, and check it against $\sqrt{1 + x}$.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

feedback.correct: Each derivative brings down the next lower power.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate twice, spot the pattern at 0, divide by $k!$, then check.

byKey.half: The check uses the general coefficient, so it comes last.

explain.text: The derivatives at 0 are the falling product $\alpha(\alpha - 1)\cdots$, and dividing by $k!$ gives the binomial coefficient. For a whole number $\alpha$ the product hits 0 and the series stops. For $\alpha = \tfrac12$ it gives the $-\tfrac18$ you found in lesson 5.

items.question: Write the first three non-zero terms of the series for $\sin 2x$, simplified.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise the whole of $2x$ to each power: $(2x)^3 = 8x^3$.

byKey.times-two: You doubled the series for $\sin x$. That is $2\sin x$, not $\sin 2x$.
byKey.power-only: Only the $x$ got the power. $(2x)^3 = 8x^3$ and $(2x)^5 = 32x^5$.
byKey.sign: The signs alternate as in $\sin u$.

items.prose: A pricing library computes $e$ as $P_n(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \tfrac{1}{k!}$ and needs an error below 0.001.
items.question: What is the smallest $n$ that does it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $P_n(1)$ for $n = 4, 5, 6$ and compare with 2.718282.

explain.text: The errors are 0.0099, 0.0016 and 0.00023 for $n = 4$, 5 and 6. Each new term divides the error by roughly the next whole number. So $n = 6$ is the first below 0.001.

items.prose: A 3-year bond pays a 6% annual coupon on £100.00 face and yields 6%, so it prices at £100.00.
items.question: What is its convexity $C = P''(y)/P$, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum $t(t + 1)\,CF_t\,(1.06)^{-t-2}$ over $t = 1, 2, 3$, then divide by £100.00.

byKey.halved: You halved it. The half belongs in the price formula, not in $C$.
byKey.duration: 2.67 is the modified duration. Convexity uses $t(t + 1)$ and one more power of 1.06.

explain.text: The terms are $2 \times 6 / 1.06^3 = 10.08$, $6 \times 6 / 1.06^4 = 28.52$ and $12 \times 106 / 1.06^5 = 950.51$. Their sum 989.10 over £100.00 gives $C = 9.89$. Short bonds have little convexity; this one's is under half that of the 5-year bond.

items.prose: A trader is long 500 options and has hedged away the delta, so $\Delta = 0$ for the book. Each option has gamma 0.08 per £1.00. Time decay costs the book £60.00 a day.
items.question: How large a daily share move, either way, does the trader need to break even? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\Delta = 0$ the P&L is $500 \times \tfrac12\Gamma\,\delta S^2$. Set it equal to £60.00.

byKey.no-root: 3 is $\delta S^2$. Take the square root.
byKey.no-half: You left out the half on the gamma term.
byKey.one-option: That is for one option. The book holds 500.

explain.text: The gamma P&L is $500 \times \tfrac12 \times 0.08\,\delta S^2 = 20\,\delta S^2$. Setting $20\,\delta S^2 = 60$ gives $\delta S^2 = 3$, so about £1.73 either way. Smaller daily moves lose money to time decay; larger ones make it.

items.question: Write the first three terms of the series for $\ln(1 - x)$.

widget.label: First three terms of ln(1 - x)

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Replace each $x$ with $-x$: $(-x)^2 = x^2$ and $(-x)^3 = -x^3$.

byKey.unchanged: That is $\ln(1 + x)$. Replace each $x$ with $-x$.
byKey.factorials: The log series divides by $k$, not $k!$.

explain.text: $(-x) - \tfrac{(-x)^2}{2} + \tfrac{(-x)^3}{3} = -x - \tfrac{x^2}{2} - \tfrac{x^3}{3}$. Every term is negative, as $\ln(1 - x) < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$.

items.title: Duration and convexity of a zero-coupon bond
items.prompt: A 10-year zero-coupon bond pays £100.00 at maturity and yields 5% a year, so $P(y) = 100(1 + y)^{-10}$. (a) Find $P'(y)$ and $P''(y)$, and show that $D = \dfrac{10}{1 + y}$ and $C = \dfrac{110}{(1 + y)^2}$. (b) Compute $P$, $D$ and $C$ at $y = 5\%$. (c) Estimate the price after a 1% rise and after a 1% fall, first with duration alone, then with duration plus convexity. Compare each with the true price, in £ to 2 decimal places. (d) Explain why the bond gains more than it loses, and name the term that would close most of the gap that is left.
items.model:
**(a) Derivatives.** Write $P(y) = 100(1 + y)^{-10}$.

$$P'(y) = -1000(1 + y)^{-11} \quad \text{(power rule and chain rule)}$$

$$P''(y) = 11000(1 + y)^{-12} \quad \text{(again: } (-10)(-11) = 110\text{)}$$

Divide by $P(y) = 100(1 + y)^{-10}$:

$$D = -\frac{P'}{P} = \frac{1000(1 + y)^{-11}}{100(1 + y)^{-10}} = \frac{10}{1 + y}, \qquad C = \frac{P''}{P} = \frac{11000(1 + y)^{-12}}{100(1 + y)^{-10}} = \frac{110}{(1 + y)^2}.$$

**(b) Values at 5%.** $P = 100 / 1.05^{10} = 100 / 1.628895 = \text{£}61.39$ (61.3913). $D = 10 / 1.05 = 9.5238$. $C = 110 / 1.1025 = 99.7732$.

**(c) Estimates.** The duration term for $\Delta y = \pm 0.01$ is $\mp 9.5238 \times 61.3913 \times 0.01 = \mp \text{£}5.85$ (5.8468). The convexity term is $\tfrac12 \times 99.7732 \times 61.3913 \times 0.0001 = +\text{£}0.31$ (0.3063), the same sign for both moves.

| Yield | Duration only | Duration plus convexity | True price |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6% | £55.54 | £55.85 | £55.84 |
| 4% | £67.24 | £67.54 | £67.56 |

The true prices are $100 / 1.06^{10} = 55.8395$ and $100 / 1.04^{10} = 67.5564$. Duration alone is about 30p too low both times. Adding convexity leaves errors of about 1p.

**(d) Why gains beat losses.** The bond gains £6.17 when yields fall 1% but loses only £5.55 when they rise 1%. The duration terms are equal and opposite; the convexity term, $+\text{£}0.31$, is added to both. So the gain exceeds the loss by about $2 \times 0.31 = \text{£}0.61$ (true gap 0.6133). This is because $P''(y) > 0$: the price curve bends up and lies above its tangent. The remaining 1p error is the cubic term $\tfrac16 P'''(y)(\Delta y)^3$, with $P'''(y) = -132000(1 + y)^{-13} = -70002$ at 5%. It gives $\mp \text{£}0.0117$, which brings the estimates to 55.8391 and 67.5561, within a twentieth of a penny. It has the sign of $-\Delta y$, so it slightly lowers the price after a rise and raises it after a fall.

rubric.text: Divides by $P$ to show $D = \tfrac{10}{1 + y}$ and $C = \tfrac{110}{(1 + y)^2}$.
Finds the duration term $\mp\text{£}5.85$ and the duration-only prices £55.54 and £67.24.
Finds the convexity term $+\text{£}0.31$ with the half, added for both moves.
Gives the true prices £55.84 and £67.56 and compares the errors.
Explains the asymmetry: equal duration terms, the same positive convexity term, gap about £0.61, because $P'' > 0$.
Names the cubic term $\tfrac16 P'''(y)(\Delta y)^3$, about $\mp\text{£}0.01$, as what closes the gap.
